title: A Framework for Evidence-Based Psychotherapy with AI (EBP-AI)
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems and large language models (LLMs) offer substantial potential to augment or even fundamentally change elements of psychological assessment and treatment. However, current AI technologies have yet to demonstrate the capacity to effect meaningful and sustained clinical change. This gap reflects both the limited integration of clinical science knowledge into language models and applications built using them, as well as the mismatch between the brief, minutes-long nature of most AI interactions and the months-long course of most evidence-based treatments. Here we introduce the Evidence-Based Psychotherapy with AI (EBP-AI) framework, which articulates a set of principles for developing effective clinical AI applications: 1) psychodiagnostic assessment, 2) longitudinal case conceptualization, 3) appropriately dosed intervention planning, 4) meaningful progress evaluation, 5) rigorous validation with clinical populations, 6) attention to real world implementation and use, 7) clinically appropriate style, and 8) understanding clinical psychology as a living science. We introduce a set of key technical questions for the development and evaluation of clinical LLMs and AIs aligned with these principles. Despite their potential, current clinical AIs fall short, in part due to issues with memory, sycophancy, and prioritizing short-term helpfulness over long-term clinical impact. Responsible and ethical design of effective, clinical-science-based AI systems will require understanding their limitations and strategically extending their capabilities.

title: Moderating effects of identity state and social dominance orientation on the relationship of status-based stressor exposure with self-reported health
description: Although clarity on the social environment’s role in health disparities is growing, knowledge gaps remain regarding factors driving heterogeneity in the effects of social stressors on life course health. Identity-related characteristics, often unmeasured, may contribute to this variability and offer novel targets for public health intervention. We assessed whether two identity-related paradigms—identity vitality, a novel modifiable characteristic capturing inclusive versus exclusive self-concept, perceived intrinsic worth, and compassionate orientation (per the Identity Vitality-Pathology (IVP) model), and social dominance orientation (SDO)—moderated the effect of financial strain on health. Using 2025 data from 2,008 non-Hispanic Black and White adults, multivariable ordinal logistic regressions with interactions showed that among men under high financial strain, greater identity vitality and higher SDO were associated with higher self-rated health, whereas effects were weak or absent in women. Findings support the IVP hypothesis that modifiable identity factors can buffer stress-related health effects, with notable gender differences.

title: Open Pilot Trial of a Single Session Consultation Service for Clients at StrongMinds Uganda
description: The need for mental health services in Sub-Saharan Africa far exceeds the availability of support, creating long waitlists for the few services that are in place. To address this crisis, implementing evidence-based, single-session interventions for individuals seeking treatment may provide timely relief. StrongMinds—a mental health charity organization serving youth and adults in Uganda—piloted a Single-Session Consultation (SSC) service for new treatment-seekers with elevated depressive symptoms, as indicated by a score on a screener survey suggesting the presence of at least mild depression. To optimize its reach and fit with StrongMinds’ service delivery model, the SSC was delivered by trained lay providers in both individual and group-based formats. Within two months (September-October 2023), the SSC was delivered to 200 Ugandan adults with elevated depression symptoms (ages 16-86; 73% female) upon initial outreach for StrongMinds’ group psychotherapy services. SSC clients reported significant improvements in hopelessness and depression symptoms at 2-week (ds = -0.73, -1.12) and 1-month follow-ups (ds = -0.96, -1.44), while waiting for group psychotherapy. SSC clients reported high SSC satisfaction (M = 4.47/5), and intervention effects did not significantly differ by delivery format (i.e., individual vs. group format). Results suggest the SSC’s acceptability, feasibility, and utility as a low-intensity, scalable intervention for adolescents and adults in Uganda on waiting lists for longer-term psychotherapy.

title: Mixed-method randomised controlled trial of art-based intervention on trait beauty appreciation and mental health of young adults
description: Mental health concerns among young adults are rising sharply, yet scalable, evidence-based prevention strategies remain scarce. Trait beauty appreciation is consistently associated with better well-being and mental health and can be taught, making it a promising target for intervention. However, robust evidence is lacking because prior studies have not controlled for general awareness training, participation confounding, and/or placebo effects. This pre-registered 6-week mixed-methods RCT (N = 102) tested a novel two-week art-based beauty appreciation intervention against a structurally equivalent observation training active control to isolate beauty-specific effects. Both programs were reported to be credible and enjoyable and were community-based. The intervention increased trait beauty appreciation relative to the control, with large effects (ηp² = .16), although gains returned to near-baseline at the four-week follow-up. No group differences emerged for psychological distress or mental well-being, and near-zero between-group effect sizes suggest the results do not support an added short-term mental-health benefit of beauty-focused training over the matched active control. However, both groups showed comparable temporary reductions in distress, with qualitative interview data identifying largely overlapping mechanisms related to emotion and attention regulation, enhanced awareness, changes in thinking, and increased motivation. Sensory processing sensitivity, a hypothesised moderator, did not moderate outcomes. These findings show that trait beauty appreciation can be temporarily shifted, but this shift did not contribute to mental health beyond an ingredient-rich, general, observation-based active control.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of psychosis-like visual perceptual disturbances and visual distortions in real and virtual environments
description: Visual perceptual disturbances (VPDs) encompass an array of anomalous visual experiences occurring in the presence of an external stimulus. Within this hierarchy, visual distortions (VDs)—manifesting as transient low-level alterations—are frequently reported across the psychosis spectrum. Despite VPDs’ prevalence and hypothesized role in hallucination and delusion formation, they remain poorly characterized. Free-viewing eye-tracking (ET) and immersive virtual reality (VR) may offer ecologically valid approaches to capturing and simulating these experiences; however, their application to VPD research has not been systematically evaluated. This preregistered systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD42023494593), conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, PsycArticles, PsycInfo, and Scopus for studies using free-viewing ET or immersive technology in participants aged 15–65 years across the psychosis spectrum (CHR, FEP, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder). Two independent reviewers screened 3,135 records; 38 studies with 3,846 participants met inclusion criteria. These split into 31 ET and 7 immersive studies. Reporting quality was assessed using STROBE criteria. Results reveal that most ET studies focused on medicated individuals with established psychosis. They show reductions in saccade amplitude and spatial search metrics—patterns consistent with a stable trait marker that partly correlates with positive symptom severity. Preliminary evidence suggests possible predictive relevance in CHR populations due to persistent aberrations. Immersive studies used VR exclusively, primarily with non-clinical samples, and rarely investigated VPDs or VDs directly. Both technologies remain scarcely used in research specifically targeting VPDs. Combining free-viewing ET with VR may offer a promising approach for ecologically valid assessment of VPDs and for advancing early detection across the psychosis continuum.

title: Self-Rated Health as a Prospective Predictor of Daily Symptoms and Illness Behavior
description: Objective: Self-rated health (SRH), the simple question “How would generally you rate your health?”, is one of the strongest known predictors of morbidity and mortality. Yet, it remains unclear whether this single subjective evaluation also captures more common, everyday physical health experiences. Understanding whether SRH predicts everyday physical health would enable a more precise analysis of the mediators and moderators of this relationship, thereby extending our understanding of how subjective health evaluations unfold in everyday life. The present preregistered study examined whether SRH prospectively predicts short-term physical symptoms and illness behavior in everyday life in the general population. Methods: Participants completed repeated online surveys over eight weeks, reporting their SRH, physical symptoms, illness behavior, and psychological characteristics. Results: Cross-sectional analyses showed that SRH was strongly associated with physical symptoms, beyond demographics, diagnosed health conditions, and socio-economic factors. Longitudinal cross-lagged models revealed that SRH prospectively predicted both physical symptoms and illness behavior at later follow-ups, whereas neither symptoms nor illness behavior predicted SRH at any assessment. Exploratory analyses further revealed that these effects were stronger among individuals with higher health anxiety and lower mental resilience. Conclusions: Together, these findings demonstrate that SRH captures not only long-term health risks but also short-term fluctuations in everyday physical health and illness behavior. Therefore, SRH may offer a simple tool for identifying individuals at risk for heightened physical symptoms experiences and may serve as a potential target for interventions aimed at improving everyday health.

title: Development and Validation of the Preparedness to Disclose Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Scale
description: The disclosure of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) can be a critical step in recovery by enabling access to social support, clinical intervention, and emotional validation. However, little is known about the psychological and contextual factors that shape individuals’ decisions to disclose NSSI. The present study developed and provided initial validation for the Preparedness to Disclose Nonsuicidal Self-Injury Scale (PDNS), a novel measure designed to assess individuals’ psychological readiness to disclose their experiences of NSSI. Seventy-five preliminary items were administered to 675 university students (77% female; M = 22.20 years, SD = 4.83), 64% of whom had previously disclosed their NSSI. Principal axis factoring revealed a three-factor structure (Self-Efficacy to Disclose, Interpersonal Motives, and Situational Readiness). The five highest loading items on each factor were retained, resulting in a 15-item scale that reliably differentiated individuals who had disclosed from those who had not. Evidence of measurement invariance across individuals who had or had not disclosed their NSSI supported the robustness and generalisability of the PDNS. Correlations with measures of theoretically related constructs provided support for the scale’s convergent and discriminant validity. These findings indicate that preparedness to disclose NSSI is a dynamic, multifaceted process shaped by social-cognitive factors. The PDNS provides a psychometrically sound tool for research and clinical practice, offering a framework to support safe and adaptive disclosure experiences among individuals who self-injure.

title: Multidimensional Assessment of Smartphone and Social Media Use: Links with Sleep and Mental Health
description: There is widespread concern that adolescent mental health is at risk in our “always connected” world. For example, smartphone and social media (S/SM) use around bedtime may displace sleep, putting mental health at risk. However, most research examining these relationships relies on undifferentiated measures of S/SM behaviours, with a need to move beyond oversimplistic models to advance mechanistic understanding. We surveyed 2,333 11-19-year-olds on an array of S/SM behaviours, using exploratory factor analysis to reveal three latent dimensions: (i) S/SM time (i.e., time spent on S/SM), (ii) problematic/negative S/SM use and (iii) SM platform use. Preregistered hypotheses tested whether these dimensions predicted self-reported sleep quality, and whether sleep quality would mediate any associations with depression and anxiety symptoms. Higher S/SM time and problematic/negative S/SM use predicted poorer sleep quality and higher symptoms of anxiety and depression. In contrast, SM platform use was associated with lower anxiety symptoms. As well as direct links between S/SM time and problematic/negative S/SM and depressive and anxiety symptoms, there were also indirect associations via sleep quality. The present study highlights the need for future longitudinal research to incorporate rich and multidimensional measures of S/SM alongside objective sleep assessments to robustly examine the role of sleep as a critical mediator in causal pathways to mental health.

title: Narrative identity themes in Mexican American couples’ COVID-19 stories predict social support and loneliness
description: A narrative identity approach was used to examine associations between narrative theme predictors and loneliness and perceived spousal social support outcomes. Participants (n = 135; 50% women; 73.3% Mexican American) enrolled in a longitudinal study of marital functioning wrote pandemic-related relationship challenge narratives and completed measures of loneliness and social support. Eight themes (established: affect, agency, communion, meaning-making; novel: challenge resolution, couple stress response, familismo, overriding positive regard) were quantitatively coded and used in analyses. Social support was associated with most themes for women, but few for men. Loneliness was associated with different themes by gender. This study extends the narrative identity literature by including a majority Mexican American sample, novel interpersonal themes, and loneliness and social support as outcomes.

title: Myths About Neurodiversity: A Community Perspective
description: Myths and misinformation about neurodivergent people are widespread, persistent, and potentially harmful, affecting access to diagnosis, accommodations, and support. In this community perspective, we identify and address a carefully considered selection of harmful myths about neurodivergence, drawn from an international collaboration of researchers, practitioners, and community members with lived experience. We collected 56 myths via open submission, then reviewed and organized key myths in four themes: 1) myths about causation, which commonly frame neurodivergence as preventable and assign blame to individual behaviors, most often of parents/caregivers; 2) myths about legitimacy, which question who counts as genuinely neurodivergent and deserves support; 3) myths about ability, which cast neurodivergent people as either fundamentally impaired or exceptionally gifted; and 4) myths about identity and diversity, which prescribe who can be neurodivergent based on demographic characteristics and often erase diversity within neurodivergence. Across these themes, a common thread emerges: false beliefs about neurodivergent people can affect whose experiences are validated and who receives support. We argue that effective responses require not only debunking but also prebunking strategies, media literacy and education, and the active co-production of research with neurodivergent communities.

title: Treatment access and barriers among university students experiencing mental health disorder and suicidal thoughts and behaviours in Aotearoa New Zealand
description:
Background: Despite the high prevalence of mental disorders and suicidal thoughts and behaviours in university students, relatively few students receive mental health treatment. We aimed to first, document inequities in treatment access to understand systemic barriers and second, describe self-reported barriers to formal help-seeking and treatment access. 
Methods: As part of the World Mental Health International College Surveys (WMH-ICS) initiative, 3,702 first year students completed online self-report surveys (mean response rate: 24.6%). The survey assessed: presence of common DSM-5 mental disorders, suicidal thoughts and behaviours; whether respondents had received treatment for their distress in the past 12 months; and perceived barriers to accessing treatment. Weighted prevalence estimates were calculated and data were analysed using multivariable statistical methods. 
Results: Among students who met DSM-5 criteria for a mental disorder, only 30.9% had received treatment. Among all students, those who were older, transgender, or worked part-time were more likely to have received treatment. Asian students were less likely to receive treatment than their European peers and men were less likely than woman. When considering self-reported barriers to seeking help, older students were more likely to report all barrier types and males were more likely to endorse a desire to talk to friends/family, handle the problem alone, or report uncertainty of treatment effectiveness. 
Conclusion: There is a large unmet treatment need for psychological distress among university students in Aotearoa New Zealand. Student support services need to consider targeted initiatives that challenge the perceived barriers to help-seeking and address inequities in treatment delivery.

title: The Completion Condition: Meaning Integration as a Prerequisite for Therapeutic Reorganization
description: Some patients come back to therapy for years, engage in good faith, and never get free. Insight accrues. Symptoms become manageable. The structure underneath holds, because feeling better and being reorganized are not the same event — and the literature has tended to treat them as if they were. We argue that one factor has been consistently underweighted: meaning integration, the point at which trauma finishes processing and the suffering attached to it stops being a present-tense experience and becomes a past-tense memory. We call this the Completion Condition. Until it happens, the loop built around the unresolved material stays load-bearing for the self, and relieving the symptoms leaves that structure exactly where it was. We look at what the completion event actually is, what conditions allow it, and why everyday practice rarely aims at it directly. Three falsifiable implications follow, all approachable with existing clinical research methods. Where the Experiential Coherence Index says when reorganization can happen, the Completion Condition says what it consists of once it does. This is a theoretical proposal requiring prospective validation, not a treatment protocol.

title: Impact of Web-Based Cognitive Bias Modification for Threat Interpretations on Depressive Symptoms Among Anxious Adults with Co-Occurring Depressive Symptoms
description:
Background. Co-occurrence of depressive and anxiety symptoms is common; however, the shortage of mental health professionals and high treatment costs means additions to in-person care are necessary to meet treatment needs. The present paper evaluates whether a web-based cognitive bias modification for interpretation (CBM-I) intervention intended for anxious adults—but which targets a shared cognitive mechanism of anxiety and depression—is superior to web-based psychoeducation at reducing co-occurring depressive symptoms. 
Methods. Latent growth curve modeling was used to assess for superiority of CBM-I over psychoeducation at reducing depressive symptoms among adults with elevated anxiety and depressive symptoms. Interventions were completed once weekly for five weeks with a 2-month follow-up assessment. Analyses were replicated in two separate datasets (Study 1: N = 1069; Study 2: N = 517) and employed multiple variations of CBM-I (Study 1: standard, added low-intensity coaching; Study 2: standard, shortened, added self-referential content, added psychoeducation). 
Results. Study 1 showed significant superiority of CBM-I over psychoeducation at post-intervention (between-group d = 0.31); this was not replicated in Study 2, but the pattern of effect sizes was similar (d = 0.21). Both interventions showed significant reductions in depressive symptoms at post-intervention (within-group ds from baseline = 0.59-0.92) that were maintained at 2-month follow-up (ds from baseline = 0.75-1.04). 
Conclusions. The current core CBM-I intervention, designed to target experiences of anxiety, appears preliminarily to be effective in reducing co-occurring depressive symptoms, though its effectiveness is not consistently superior to that of psychoeducation and needs replication in randomized trials.

title: Female Beauty Ideals in the Digital Age: A Structural Equation Model of the Impact of Social Media Pressure on Body Image and Disordered Eating
description: y image research has primarily focused on the effects of social media platform usage; however, it has largely overlooked the impact of social media pressures through the lens of gender roles. The present study employed structural equation modelling to examine the effect of social media pressure on body image concerns and examined the power of beauty standards related to gender roles to explain this relationship. A total of 393 female social media users completed measures assessing social media use frequency, social media pressure, internalization of beauty standards, social physique anxiety, self-esteem and disordered eating. Outcomes revealed that social media pressures directly predict disordered eating, with additional indirect effects through internalization of the thinness ideal (associated with the female role). In contrast, internalization of the muscular ideal (associated with the male role) did not explain this relationship. Notably, the study examined a model in which women who reported greater social media pressure and greater internalization of the thinness ideal also exhibited higher levels of social physique anxiety and lower self-esteem, both of which were associated with greater disordered eating. These findings expand understanding of social media pressure and offer valuable insight for prevention and intervention targeting body image-related disorders.

title: Maladaptive AI Use for Learning: A Regulatory-Failure Framework, Scale Development, Nomological Network, and Links to Reduced Learning Outcomes
description: Generative AI can support learning, but it may become counterproductive when learners use it to bypass regulatory processes needed for durable understanding. We conceptualise this pattern as maladaptive AI use for learning, a learning-specific regulatory failure within self-regulated learning comprising Uncritical Reliance, Shallow Processing, and Illusory Competence. Across six studies (N = 909), we advanced a regulatory-failure framework, developed and validated a 12-item measure, mapped its nomological network, and examined links with learning outcomes. Study 1 generated and content-validated the initial item pool. Study 2 identified a three-factor structure through EFA. Studies 3 and 4 confirmed this structure, with robust factor loadings and good internal consistency across validation studies (αs = .86–.90). Study 4 supported sex invariance, convergent and discriminant validity. In Study 4, maladaptive AI use for learning was associated with higher AI attachment, social influence surrounding AI adoption, positive attitudes toward AI, academic procrastination, controlled academic motivation, trait anxiety, and maladaptive coping, as well as lower critical thinking in AI use, open-mindedness, and conscientiousness. Study 5 showed good one-week test–retest reliability (ICC(2,1) = .77). Study 6 supported criterion validity, with greater maladaptive AI use for learning predicting lower GPA, poorer independent writing-task performance after AI-supported learning, and greater overconfidence in perceived understanding relative to actual performance. These findings clarify maladaptive AI use for learning as a distinct learning-specific construct and provide a foundation for future research and instructional interventions that help learners use AI to support rather than replace the regulatory processes required for durable learning.

title: Children’s use of social networking sites and their mental health and wellbeing: A longitudinal study
description: Immersed within a digital age, children aged 7-to-12 years old are engaging online. Despite the age restrictions of social networking sites (SNS) averaging 13 years, these are easy to bypass and children are using them (Ofcom, 2025; Woodhouse & Lalic, 2024). Online behaviours have been widely linked to positive and negative outcomes for adolescence. This study aims to investigate children’s behaviours on SNS and whether these predict self-esteem, wellbeing, and mental health outcomes over time. A sample of 258 7-to-12-year-olds completed a longitudinal online survey over two time points (six months apart) measuring time spent online, online self-disclosure, self-presentation, bonding and bridging social capital, self-esteem, wellbeing, and mental health (anxiety and depression). Findings demonstrate that being male predicted higher self-esteem over a six month period. Further, bonding social capital and using a range of self-presentation techniques predicted poorer mental health over a six month period. No SNS behaviours predicted wellbeing over a six-month period, although older children reported better wellbeing. Results are discussed in terms of the association between children’s SNS behaviours and their social-emotional development.

title: Navigating the unknown: The sociocultural and metacognitive architecture of wisdom
description: Psychological wisdom research has shifted from characterizing rare exemplars and desired outcomes to specifying processes that support sound judgment under uncertainty. Yet it has advanced along two siloed tracks: research on folk theories—cultural tools such as exemplars,  narratives, heuristics (including proverbs and maxims), and standards of judgment—and on scientific models of mechanisms involved in wise judgment. This review bridges these research tracks using a situated metacognitive lens: folk theories provide candidate attributes or strategies for action, whereas perspectival metacognition—the capacity to recognize epistemic limits, coordinate viewpoints, and track uncertainty and change—regulates their context-sensitive selection and use. We synthesize evidence connecting wisdom-related processes to emotional balance, relational well-being, cooperation, and reduced polarization, while noting boundary conditions. We show how this synthesis sharpens measurement trade-offs, highlighting limits of global self-report and advances in situated assessment. Finally, we summarize work on wisdom development and cultivation, and consider socio-ecological implications in an AI-shaped world.

title: Daydreaming in the Age of Self-Identified ADHD: Revisiting the Short Imaginal Processes Inventory in US and Hong Kong Adolescents
description: Emerging social media environments have contributed to a growing group of adolescents who self-identify with ADHD, reframing ADHD from a strictly clinical category into a socially meaningful identity. This identity may shape how adolescents interpret mind wandering and respond to daydreaming measures. Because such meanings are embedded in cultural narratives, adolescents may show culture-specific endorsement patterns. Therefore, validating the factor structure of daydreaming among this population and establishing measurement invariance across cultures are important for supporting the cross-cultural validity of the Short Imaginal Processes Inventory (SIPI; Huba et al., 1981). We tested the SIPI’s three-factor structure and measure invariance in 666 adolescents from the United States (n = 452, Mage = 15.50, SD = 1.33) and Hong Kong (n = 214, Mage = 15.70, SD = 1.16). Subscales showed good to excellent internal consistency (α = .76–.94). Confirmatory factor and measurement invariance analyses supported the SIPI’s three-factor structure and cross-cultural comparability among self-identified ADHD adolescents.

title: Cognitive Modeling of Autobiographical Memory Test: Theoretical Approach to the Mechanisms of Overgeneral Memory
description: Overgeneral autobiographical memory is a well-known transdiagnostic feature of psychopathology, commonly assessed using the Autobiographical Memory Test (AMT), a cued recall method. AMT performance has been scored using heterogeneous outcome measures across studies, including differences in whether specific or general memories are treated as the primary outcome and in how omission responses are handled, raising concerns about replicability. In the present study, we propose a model–based scoring framework for the AMT, termed the accessibility model, which decomposes memory retrieval into three latent parameters: accessibility of specific memories (ρ), accessibility of general memories (γ), and the probability of initiating additional retrieval following goal-incongruent memory retrieval (φ). We firstly conducted simulation studies to examine model behavior and estimation stability, demonstrating that reliable parameter estimation requires approximately 15 trials (cue words) per condition. Next, we tested theoretically derived predictions using three empirical datasets. Results showed that concrete cues yielded higher ρ values, whereas abstract cues yielded higher γ values, consistent with theories of cue-driven accessibility. Instructional manipulations showed that traditional instructions emphasizing specific retrieval goals (AMT-TI), relative to minimal instructions that allowed reporting of any memory (AMT-MI), increased φ. Retrieval instructions also modulated memory accessibility, yielding higher ρ and lower γ in AMT-TI than AMT-MI. Furthermore, depressive symptom severity was associated with higher γ and lower φ for negative cues, indicating heightened accessibility of negative overgeneral memories and reduced likelihood of initiating further retrieval. We highlight several avenues for future refinement of the model and its broader theoretical implications.

title: Developing an open multi-domain assessment battery using laboratory tasks for children in low- and middle-income countries
description: Recent years have seen growing interest in field research using randomized designs to evaluate the impacts of interventions on early child development in low- and middle-income countries. Measuring these impacts requires assessments that can track development prior to school entry in settings that are often noisy and outdoors. Drawing from research in developmental cognitive science, we created an open multi-domain assessment battery for testing children in low- and middle-income countries consisting of tasks based on experimental paradigms used in laboratory settings. These tasks were designed to target abilities that emerge across cultures early in life and predict later performance on related skills in adulthood. This battery was administered to 1435 Ghanaian children whose parent previously took part in a randomized controlled field experiment on the impacts of parent secondary education on their children, measuring performance on tasks at ages 1.5, 3.5, 5.5, and 7.5 years. Starting at age 3.5, children’s responses to the tasks were internally consistent and above chance, with overall test results predictive of later performance. There was strong evidence of validity both for tasks in numeracy and spatial reasoning, which were designed to tap into culturally invariant cognitive capacities, as well as those in language and executive functioning, which required more context-specific adaptation. In contrast, there was little evidence of validity in infant tasks or tasks focused on intuitive physics or mental state reasoning. Nevertheless, our results suggest that our approach to assessment design is effective at producing tasks that are internally consistent and sensitive to individual differences within cohort. By making our testing materials and data freely accessible, we hope to provide a foundation for the development of tools for studying cognitive development in field settings.

title: Action Simulation as an Intervention to Improve Balance, Mobility and Gait in Healthy Older Adults: A Scoping Review
description: Falls in older adults are a significant public health concern. Action simulation interventions involving action observation and/or motor imagery have been proposed as alternative or adjunct strategies to physical exercise for reducing fall risk. These approaches may minimize barriers to physical practice and may specifically target deficits in motor planning that are linked to falls. The purpose of this scoping review is to examine how action simulation interventions have been applied and evaluated in healthy older adults, and assess their effectiveness in improving balance, mobility, and gait. A systematic search of six databases and repositories was conducted. Studies were included if they used action simulation interventions in healthy, community-dwelling adults aged 60+ years and examined movement outcomes related to balance, gait or functional mobility. Nineteen studies with 587 older adults were included. Motor imagery was the most common action simulation intervention (n = 11 [58%]), and most studies were randomized controlled trials (n = 14 [74%]). Only one study examined long-term effects on balance and gait performance (i.e., 1-month post-intervention). The examined outcomes varied widely, including static and dynamic balance, gait, and mobility. Most interventions (n = 17 [71%]) reported significant improvement in at least one domain, but findings were inconsistent across studies, and none assessed intervention implementability. Overall, this review highlights some promising effects of action simulation on balance, mobility and gait in older adults. However, if action simulation techniques are to be adopted as a fall prevention strategy, more studies examining acceptability are needed.

title: Aesthetic Emotions and the Drive for Knowledge
description:
In this paper, I address how the arts contribute to knowledge and understanding by defending an Affective Aesthetic Cognitivism (AAC). AAC is an empirically informed theory model, concerning the role of affect and emotions in sustaining the transformative, cognitive impact of the arts.  The relation of our art engagement to our drive for knowledge might at times seem rather indirect. We do not mainly engage with art for educational purposes but rather for pleasure (e.g., when we rewatch a movie or TV show we love) or for emotion regulation (e.g., when we go to an art exhibition when we are bored). Aesthetic Cognitivism in philosophy and psychology, in contrast, focuses on the epistemic outcomes of our art engagement. It provides a theory about the value of the arts not “as sources of delight, amusement, pleasure, or emotional catharsis, but as sources of understanding.” (Brewer 2025, 1). The proposed AAC in this chapter goes one step further by integrating affect and cognition, arguing that the emotions are not a byproduct but a significant driver of the epistemic impact of the arts. The claim of AAC is therefore not just that the emotions accompany epistemic changes, or that they motivate cognitive engagement (they do that as well), but that specific aesthetic emotions play a constitutive role in how understanding through the arts is achieved. 
	I first discuss the more general impact of art and cultural artifacts on our habits of perceiving and distinguish them from epistemically valuable cognitive gains; this gives me the opportunity to revisit some central claims of Aesthetic Cognitivism. I then examine how affect and cognition have been related in aesthetic psychology and, starting with Berlyne’s (1960, 1970) work on curiosity that recent psychology has been amended to cover more specific emotions. title: Who eats bugs, and what does it say about them? Disgust, stereotyping, and the social construction of the insect consumer
description: The promotion of edible insects as a sustainable source of protein has gained considerable attention. However, consumer resistance remains high in Western countries, driven by disgust, food neophobia, and cultural taboos. Quantitative research has addressed the individual-level barriers to insect consumption, whilst the social and cultural meanings of entomophagy and its practitioners are under-explored, particularly in Central European contexts. The present study explored how Polish adults perceive insect-eating as a dietary practice, how they socially categorise and stereotype insect-eaters, and what psychological and sociocultural mechanisms underlie resistance to entomophagy. Semi-structured face-to-face interviews were conducted with 19 Polish adults (15F, 4M; age range 19–62 years) in August 2025. Data were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis from a constructivist epistemological position. The findings suggest that social and political factors shape dietary rules and have implications for how we design culturally sensitive ways to encourage people to adopt them, and that resistance to certain types of food operates as a form of social categorisation, in which disgust can be transferred from food to its consumer. This approach to analysis allowed for an exploration of how individual barriers, such as disgust, may be transformed and reinforced by social processes and political polarisation. The study suggests that resistance to insect-based food was not organised solely around knowledge. Participants often recognised nutritional or ecological arguments, but still rejected insects because they were associated with disgust, contamination, social deviance, political meanings, and threats to familiar food identity. The study shows that insect-based foods may be rejected not only because they are unfamiliar, but also as markers through which consumers are socially imagined and evaluated.

title: Embodied empathy towards patients with stroke
description:
Empathy toward patients with stroke may facilitate helping. Because stroke patients’ physical disabilities impact multiple body parts causing context-dependent difficulties during everyday activities, observers need to continuously monitor these difficulties to update their empathic responses. Here we tested whether observers embody the stroke patients’ motor difficulties during everyday locomotory task, and whether time-variable empathetic responses are coupled with helping motivation, 

Participants viewed videos of patients with stroke or healthy individuals walking and stepping over obstacles. In study 1, we measured participants’ bodily sensations, emotions felt while viewing the videos, and emotions attributed to the patient in the video. In study 2, participants provided continuously rated empathy and willingness to help while viewing the same videos. Participants attributed strong limb sensations to the patients’ stroke-affected body parts, and mirrored these sensations also in their own bodies. They also experienced and attributed stronger negative emotional experiences to the patients than healthy controls. Time-varying ratings revealed that empathy and willingness to help toward patients were engaged even before the difficulties in locomotion were evident. Empathy and willingness to help ratings also increased continuously over time and were strongly coupled.

These findings suggest that empathy toward patients with stroke is embodied, through sensations specific to the stroke-affected limbs and bodily regions. Empathy and helping motivation are rapidly engaged, dynamically updated as situations unfold, and tightly coupled over time. Overall these results suggest an embodied basis of empathy toward patients with stroke and its close relationship with helping motivation.

title: Measuring Depression Literacy: Development and Psychometric Validation of the Multifaceted Depression Literacy Scale (M-DL)
description: Depression Literacy is a multifaceted construct encompassing the knowledge needed to recognize and effectively respond to symptoms of depression. This study aimed to develop and validate a self-report questionnaire measuring depression literacy and to evaluate its factorial structure, as well as its criterion, convergent, and discriminant validity. Using a 56-item pool from existing studies, we conducted secondary analyses of two representative German adult surveys (ages 18–69; N = 5,178 and 5,285) to develop the Multifaceted Depression Literacy Scale  (M-DL). Development proceeded in five steps: expert rating of the item pool, exploratory factor analysis and item selection (first survey), calculation of psychometric properties, confirmatory factor analysis, and evaluation of construct and discriminant validity (second survey). To assess validity, scores were compared across subgroups with different depression contact (none, indirect, or personal) and correlated with a self-rated depression knowledge item and the Depression Stigma Scale. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a 14-factor, multidimensional M-DL structure. Criterion validity was shown by significant score differences between professionals or relatives and individuals with no depression contact (both p < .05). Convergent validity with the self-assessment item was low but significant (p < .05), and discriminant validity was supported by negative correlations with Personal and Perceived Stigma (p < .001). We developed a brief self-assessment instrument for depression literacy covering all literature-based facets except prevention, and demonstrated its factorial, criterion, and discriminant validity. The instrument showed good psychometric properties and may help identify individuals or groups with low depression literacy. title: “Glimmers of Hope”: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Unconditional Perinatal Cash Transfers and Maternal Hope
description: Unconditional child cash transfer programs are implemented to reduce economic hardship, yet little is known about their effects on positive psychological capacities that support well-being, such as hope. This mixed-methods study examined associations between exposure to Rx Kids – a universal and unconditional perinatal cash transfer program – and maternal hope. Survey data from 966 mothers were analyzed using a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences design. Mothers exposed to Rx Kids were significantly more likely (p<0.05) to report feeling hopeful, being hopeful about life, and maintaining hope in difficult times. Thematic analysis of interviews with 46 enrolled mothers indicated increased stability, greater capacity to think ahead, and enhanced confidence in navigating parenting and everyday life. Findings suggest that hope is a malleable psychological resource that may be strengthened through upstream economic interventions, underscoring the value of incorporating positive psychological functioning into evaluations of social policy.

title: Including social network quality in public health research: a scoping review on current practices
description:
Aim: To (1) provide insight into how social network quality can be included in public health research and (2) generate directions for future research concerning the conceptualization and measurement of social network quality. 

Methods: A pre-registered scoping review using PubMed and APA PsychInfo as information sources. Sources of evidence were deemed eligible if they were full-text articles and reported on conceptualization and/or measurement of social network quality in public health research concerning humans. 

Results: In total, 78 articles were included. For most articles, the possible conceptualization used (if any) could only be implied based on the aspects that are measured in the reported studies. There is a large heterogeneity in aspects, with some recurring frequently (e.g., support, specific relationships, and satisfaction). This is indicative of differences in researchers’ conceptualization of social network quality.

Conclusion: The point of departure for future research is to advance the conceptualization of social network quality. The diversity in current conceptualizations and measurements of social network quality in public health research can even be beneficial. However, to benefit from this epistemic diversity, researchers need to make their conceptualizations and measurements explicit – and share them with others.

title: Beyond the Present Moment: Why Mindfulness Research Needs a Historical Perspective
description: Background: Mindfulness research has drawn extensively on the construct's long textual record for conceptual definitions but rarely treated that record as a source of empirical evidence. As a result, contemporary work captures cross-sectional variation across present-day populations without addressing the longer historical trajectories that produced it, leaving open questions about how cultural and ecological forces have shaped mindfulness over centuries and millennia. Objective: This paper develops the case for a historical psychology of mindfulness, positioned between evolutionary work on phylogenetic timescales and cross-cultural work on contemporary populations. Methods: It reviews methodological approaches that make diachronic analysis tractable, including top-down dictionary construction, bottom-up emic curation, distributed and contextualized construct representation, large language model prompting, and generative simulation with historical large language models, and surveys source materials across canonical and commentarial traditions, practical and instructional literature, first-person accounts, general published text, and non-textual cultural artefacts. Results: Drawing on cross-cultural psychology, the paper outlines the construct, method, and item biases that the temporal dimension compounds. Conclusion: It closes with three questions for a research agenda: how mindfulness is distributed across populations, what shapes it, and whether contemplative traditions converged on a shared phenomenon.

title: Assessing chronic pain processes longitudinally: Validation of the German “Assessing Chronic Pain Processes” (ProCEss) item set
description:
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) has become increasingly feasible with technological advances, capturing dynamic fluctuations in symptoms and processes. EMA is ecologically valid and can reduce recall biases. However, there is a lack of thoroughly validated items. 
Therefore, the “Prozesse Chronischer Schmerzen ErfaSSen” (ProCEss; engl. „Assessing Chronic Pain Processes”) item set was developed for an EMA coverage model, i.e. a broad range of the day shall be captured instead of single momentary experiences. In multiple studies, practitioners (n = 18 + n = 12) and affected persons (n = 12 + n = 12) contributed to establishing content validity through an adapted Discriminant Content Validity Method and Cognitive Interviews. Findings from these studies informed the development of written and audio-visual comprehensibility aids, designed and evaluated in a healthy sample (n = 128) to replace extensive participant instruction procedures.
Across studies, both affected persons and practitioners rated the items positively with regard to comprehensibility and relevance. Feedback of affected persons contributed to item refinement, and the item set was reduced from 29 to 25 items. The evaluation of the comprehensibility aids further supported the comprehensibility of the item set in general.
The ProCEss item set is among the first validated instruments for assessing chronic pain processes using EMA in German. The current study supports its relevance and comprehensibility. Other forms of validity have to be established in future research, and comprehensiveness might be enhanced by future extensions of the item set.

title: Calibration of retrospective and prospective life satisfaction judgments around the world
description: It is a physical fact that humans have access to records of the past but not of the future and that this creates an epistemic asymmetry in time. We explore the epistemic asymmetry, hypothesizing that retrospection about past psychological states is less biased than prospection about future states. Leveraging data from the Pew Research Center’s Global Attitudes Project, involving 61,271 participants across 34 countries, we examined the calibration and bias of individuals' assessments of past and future life satisfaction relative to present assessments. A multi-method analysis contrasted individual and national-level evaluations of life satisfaction across two waves, five years apart, with numerous control variables to account for potential confounding factors. Results confirmed miscalibration in prospective judgments of future life satisfaction, whereas retrospective judgments of past life satisfaction showed no meaningful miscalibration. This supports a psychological effect of the physical arrow of time on human judgment, robust across diverse samples worldwide.

title: Interbrain synchrony analysis for fNIRS –  a signal processing primer
description: Interbrain synchrony (IBS), also referred to as interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), has become a central construct in social neuroscience and beyond. It describes the temporal alignment of neural activity across individuals and has been studied in a range of paradigms, including sequential interactions, shared-stimulus settings, and hyperscanning, i.e., the simultaneous neuroimaging of two or more individuals during real-time interaction. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is increasingly used for such studies because it supports portable, naturalistic, face-to-face paradigms. A central goal in these experiments is to quantify IBS between interacting individuals. Wavelet transform coherence (WTC) has become the most widely used method for estimating IBS in fNIRS studies. However, its application involves several non-trivial signal-processing assumptions and time–frequency trade-offs that are often not explicitly addressed, making it difficult to apply and interpret the method consistently. Reliable estimation of IBS is crucial not only for experimental design but also for the interpretation and comparison of results within and across studies. Here, we aim to support this endeavor by providing a principled overview of the relevant signal-processing foundations. To enable researchers to make informed methodological choices, the paper first introduces key concepts in time–frequency analysis and clarifies their relation to WTC. These principles are then connected to the analysis of IBS in fNIRS datasets, with particular emphasis on the time–frequency constraints inherent to wavelet-based methods. Building on these foundations, we provide practical recommendations for experiment design, preprocessing, and frequency targeting. By making resolution limits and analysis assumptions explicit, this primer aims to support improved study planning and more consistent interpretation of IBS in the rapidly growing field of fNIRS-based investigations and beyond.
